name: Chronotype–Schedule Fit
definition: The degree of fit between an individual’s preferred biological timing and externally required schedules.
representationScale: continuous or ordinal level; clinically meaningful thresholds only where validated
polarityDirection: Higher values = greater chronotype–schedule alignment.
mechanism: Mismatch can produce chronic sleep curtailment and repeated circadian misalignment.
likelyDownstreamInfluences: Lower alertness at required times, sleep debt, and potentially poorer cognitive/health outcomes.
moderatorsBoundaryConditions: Evidence for specific cognitive effects is heterogeneous and often observational.
typicalInteractionCandidates: Interacts with age, work schedules, light exposure, family obligations, and technology use.
timeScaleQualifier: Repeated mismatch or persistent social jetlag may continue chronically; adaptation rate varies with schedule and context.
persistenceRecovery: Commonly persists across Days–chronic; recovery depends on cause, dose, and intervention.
measurementAssessmentMethods: See linked Operationalizations records.
measurementCaveats: Indicators may be state-, protocol-, dose-, and population-dependent; do not equate a single proxy with the construct. Chronotype is not a personality type and does not dictate behavior.
evidenceNotes: May affect when people are most receptive to learning, persuasion, complex decisions, or behavior-change demands. Chronotype is not a personality type and does not dictate behavior.
commonMisinterpretations: Chronotype is not a personality type and does not dictate behavior.

name: Circadian Timing Alignment
definition: The degree of alignment between internal circadian phase and the timing of sleep, work, meals, light exposure, and required behavior.
representationScale: continuous or ordinal level; clinically meaningful thresholds only where validated
polarityDirection: Higher values = greater circadian alignment.
mechanism: Circadian timing alters arousal, temperature, hormonal rhythms, sleep propensity, and cognitive performance independent of time awake.
likelyDownstreamInfluences: Reduced alertness and cognitive performance, increased error risk, altered mood and metabolic regulation.
moderatorsBoundaryConditions: Night shift, jet lag, rotating schedules, and forced desynchrony adaptation varies.
typicalInteractionCandidates: Interacts with sleep debt, lighting, work design, meal timing, and social obligations.
persistenceRecovery: Commonly persists across Hours–weeks; recovery depends on cause, dose, and intervention.
measurementAssessmentMethods: See linked Operationalizations records.
measurementCaveats: Indicators may be state-, protocol-, dose-, and population-dependent; do not equate a single proxy with the construct. Shift work includes social and structural factors beyond circadian physiology.
evidenceNotes: Can make the same behavioral demand substantially harder at biological night timing of interventions and critical decisions matters. Shift work includes social and structural factors beyond circadian physiology.

mechanism: Gives the less dependent actor bargaining leverage and changes compliance, exit, and conflict options.
moderatorsBoundaryConditions: Legitimacy, task relevance, culture, hierarchy stability, accountability, dependence, and formal versus informal authority.
persistenceRecovery: Usually persistent within a stable group but can change abruptly after turnover, failure, or reallocation.

measurementCaveats: Power, status, reputation, authority, and centrality are distinct; rankings are relation- and domain-specific.
evidenceNotes: Scientifically defensible with substantial supporting literature, while construct boundaries, causal identification, measurement, or transferability remain context dependent. Representative records: SRC228; SRC246; SRC258.
commonMisinterpretations: Treating high status as a personal essence, moral worth, or the same construct as formal office, perceived status, or social power.
